newsitem.title: MOROCCO: PRESS DIGEST - Morocco economic weeklies - Jan 31.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Morocco economic weeklies - Jan 31.

text.p: These are the leading stories in Morocco's weekly economic press. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Drafting of main outlines of next Finance Law starts, with a priority continuing to be mastering the budget deficit.
- Cost of living rose three percent in 1996, according to Statistics Office, the lowest annual rise since 1988.

- Analysts perplexed over fall in share price of Moroccan refinery Samir in which state holds nearly 70 percent and which is slated for further privatisation. The enterprise is healthy and a 'hard core' of shareholders will be announced in spring.
- Finance Minister Mohamed Kabbaj pushes for a reduction of interest rates for small- and medium-sized enterprises even if it hits margins of smaller banks.

- Economy registers positive results amid social unease caused by university disruptions and the one-day strike in the main agriculture fund (CNCA). According to Population Minister Lamine Benomar, Morocco will benefit from growth in 1997, in the meantime, Morocco prepares its programme to upgrade the economy which is due for completion in February.

- Morocco's Office Cherifien des Phosphates (OCP) tentative net operating results are estimated at 800 million dirhams ($87 million) in 1996. The pickup is attributed to the rise of phosphates prices on the world markets and new orientations of the company, but retained losses stand at 2.1 billion dirhams. Managing director Mourad Cherif says it will need two years to drain off the deficit if the market keeps an upward trend.

- Businessmen with headquarters in Ain Sebaa, industrial district of Casablanca which represents upto 25 percent of the country's industrial output and employs 50,000 workers, complain about poor infrastructure. They deplore state of roads and increasing number of shantytowns.
- Casablanca port new terminal makes it the first port in Africa. In 1996, it took over 37 percent of maritime traffic nationwide.
